::: {.paper-status}
SSRN preprint · September 2026 · DOI [10.2139/ssrn.7445120](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7445120) (listed on SSRN under Yang Liu)
:::

::: {.standfirst}
Two factor models can give every stock exactly the same fitted return and still disagree about how much of it comes from hidden factors, from observed factors such as the market, and from an intercept that no factor explains. This paper shows that a convention sets the split: the ruler, which decides when two characteristics, such as two value signals, count as overlapping. Because the ruler is estimated from the same data, its estimation error belongs in the standard errors. In a stylised simulation with 960 time periods, built to isolate this mechanism, leaving that error out makes intervals meant to contain the true value 95 times in 100 contain it only about 89–92 times <span class="loc" title="Paper, Table II, p. 34">(Table II, p. 34)</span>.
:::

## The question {#the-question}

In the agenda, this paper follows [Geometric Framework](/research/geometric-framework.html) and asks: once the ruler is chosen, what does it decide, and how precisely? The next paper, [Interpreting Pricing Errors](/research/interpreting-pricing-errors.html), asks what a smaller alpha then means.

**When a factor model built on firm characteristics fits returns, what decides how much of the fit it credits to hidden factors, to observed factors such as the market, and to the intercept? And how precisely can that split be measured?**

The model has three parts. Besides hidden factors (common drivers it infers from the data) and observed factors such as the market, there is the intercept: the part of expected return that no factor in this model explains (the home page's "alpha" is a close relative, measured against a stated benchmark model). You can move part of the fit from the intercept or the market into the hidden factors, adjust the hidden factors to compensate, and leave every fitted return exactly as it was. Every such split fits equally well, so the fit itself cannot choose among them. A convention decides it: the ruler. Characteristics also differ in scale and overlap, even after each is standardised <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 1, p. 2">(Section 1, p. 2)</span>, so the choice of ruler matters.

::: {.ruler-block}
**Why a model needs a ruler.** To say how much of a stock's expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler. Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score. Such a weighted combination is called a direction (it is not a portfolio). The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks: how large they typically are, and whether two directions' scores line up across stocks, high on the same stocks and low on the same stocks. So the ruler is the convention a model uses to measure how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. Two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks count as overlapping under the characteristic ruler but as unrelated under the plain ruler.
:::

## Why it matters {#why-it-matters}

When researchers report how closely the hidden factors align with a benchmark, how large the intercept is, or which combinations of characteristics the hidden factors represent, each number depends on the split, not only on the fit <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 1, p. 7">(Proposition 1, p. 7)</span>.

- **Economic.** R² cannot tell these splits apart, so a smaller reported intercept may reflect the convention, not new explanatory power <span class="loc" title="Paper, Corollary 1, p. 7">(Corollary 1, p. 7)</span>.
- **Statistical.** The characteristic ruler is estimated from the same data. Treating it as known leaves out the ruler's own sampling error and the way that error moves with the noise in returns <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 1 and equation (5.8), pp. 16-17">(Theorem 1, p. 16)</span>; in the paper's simulation, this makes standard errors too small <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.2, p. 33">(Section 8.2, p. 33)</span>. State the ruler; if it is estimated, include its error.

## The argument at a glance {#the-argument-at-a-glance}

::: {.logic-map}
1. **Same fit, different split.** Two models can give every stock the same fitted return yet credit it differently to hidden factors, observed factors and an intercept <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 1, p. 7">(Proposition 1, p. 7)</span>. → [A simple example](#a-simple-example)
2. **The fit cannot decide.** Because the fits are identical, R² and residuals cannot choose between the splits <span class="loc" title="Paper, Corollary 1, p. 7">(Corollary 1, p. 7)</span>. → [Why it matters](#why-it-matters)
3. **A convention decides.** So the choice falls to a convention: the ruler <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 3.1, pp. 6-7">(Section 3.1, pp. 6–7)</span>. → [The framework](#the-framework)
4. **The ruler matters in U.S. data.** The characteristic ruler counts overlap by the stocks two characteristics pick out, and in U.S. data it differs sharply from the plain ruler <span class="loc" title="Paper, Table I, p. 31">(Table I, p. 31)</span>. → [Design and main results](#design-and-main-results)
5. **Its error counts.** Because this ruler is estimated from the same data, its error flows into every reported split, so the paper derives standard errors that include it and do not depend on how the model is parameterised <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorems 1-2, pp. 16, 20">(Theorems 1–2, pp. 16, 20)</span>. → [The framework](#the-framework)
6. **Evidence.** In a stylised simulation with 960 time periods, leaving that error out makes intervals meant to contain the true value 95 times in 100 contain it only about 89–92 times; including the error restores about 94–95 <span class="loc" title="Paper, Table II, p. 34">(Table II, p. 34)</span>. → [Design and main results](#design-and-main-results)
7. **Near a cap.** Some models, such as the Geometric Framework paper's NA-IPCA (no-arbitrage instrumented principal component analysis, named for this cap), limit how much return the intercept may carry. When the estimate sits against that limit, the cap "binds"; below it, the cap is "slack". The cap is measured with the same estimated ruler, so the ruler's error moves the cap too; the paper builds an interval that holds either way, at the cost of extra width <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 4, p. 29; Table III, p. 36">(Theorem 4, p. 29)</span>. → [Design and main results](#design-and-main-results)
:::

## The framework {#the-framework}

At each date, stock $i$ has characteristics $z_{i,t}$ and a next-period excess return. The model has three blocks <span class="loc" title="Paper, equation (2.1), p. 4">(equation 2.1, p. 4)</span>:

$$
r_{i,t+1} = z_{i,t}'\Gamma_\beta f_{t+1} + z_{i,t}'\Gamma_\delta g_{t+1} + z_{i,t}'\Gamma_\alpha + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}.
$$

Here $f$ are hidden (latent) factors, $g$ are observed factors and $\Gamma_\alpha$ sets the intercept from characteristics. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) measures two directions by the scores they give real stocks <span class="loc" title="Paper, equation (2.5), p. 5">(equation 2.5, p. 5)</span>:

$$
\langle a,b\rangle_{Q_Z} = a'Q_Z\,b = \mathbb{E}\!\left[N_t^{-1}(Z_t a)'(Z_t b)\right].
$$

The ruler "specifies a convention" for separating the blocks <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 1, p. 2">(p. 2)</span>: which ruler to use is declared, not discovered, but the characteristic ruler's values are estimated from the data. The theory makes three claims.

1. **Same fit, different split.** For any ruler, a matched change rescales the hidden-factor loadings, removes the other blocks' overlap with them, and offsets both changes in the factor series, so every fitted return is unchanged <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 1, p. 7">(Proposition 1, p. 7)</span>. A finite cap on how much the intercept may carry is different: it is not a change of ruler, and it can exclude models and change fitted returns <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 1, p. 2; Section 3.1, p. 7">(pp. 2, 7)</span>.
2. **Inference with an estimated ruler.** The estimate's large-sample expansion adds a ruler-estimation term to the usual return term, including their covariance <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 1, p. 16">(Theorem 1, p. 16)</span>. The result is one standard-error formula that includes the ruler's own error and does not depend on how the model is parameterised <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 2, p. 20">(Theorem 2, p. 20)</span>.
3. **Near an estimated cap.** The estimated ruler moves the cap as well as the estimate, so in large samples the estimate behaves like a normal draw pushed back onto a moving boundary, and its distribution is generally not symmetric <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 3, p. 26">(Theorem 3, p. 26)</span>. Intervals built from worst-case quantiles have at least nominal coverage in large samples at any distance from the cap, and may be conservative <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 4, p. 29">(Theorem 4, p. 29)</span>. The guarantee excludes reports whose critical quantile sits at an atom, such as the intercept's own size when the cap binds exactly <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 7.3, p. 28">(p. 28)</span>.

<details class="robustness">
<summary>Technical statement</summary>

- **Target.** A loading class without hidden-factor rotations, identified by local curvature <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 2, p. 8">(Proposition 2, p. 8)</span>; covariance alignment, with local regularity and a strictly slack cap, suffices to make it the structural class even with a fixed cross section <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 3, p. 12">(Proposition 3, p. 12)</span>.
- **Estimator.** Exactly profiled (each date's factors solved exactly by least squares for any candidate loadings, dates combined with fixed weights, only loadings searched), on a regular local branch <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 1, p. 16">(Theorem 1, p. 16)</span>.
- **Reports.** Each smooth report has a chart-invariant influence function <span class="loc" title="Paper, Theorem 2, p. 20">(Theorem 2, p. 20)</span>; HAC estimation gives valid intervals <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 5, p. 23">(Proposition 5, p. 23)</span>. For one constraint and a scalar report, the slack and binding endpoints suffice <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 6, p. 28">(Proposition 6, p. 28)</span>.

</details>

## A simple example {#a-simple-example}

{{< include /_includes/_exhibit-helpers.qmd >}}

An analogy. Three departments share one office, and the company's total profit is fixed. Each department's reported profit depends on how shared overhead is allocated. Change the rule and every department's number changes, but the total does not, so checking the total can never tell you which rule is right. Here the departments are the hidden factors, the observed factors and the intercept; the overhead is the overlap between characteristics that pick out the same stocks.

::: {.caveat}
**Try this.** 1. Set ρ, the overlap between the two value signals, to 0: both rulers agree. 2. Drag ρ to 0.9: the hidden-factor part grows, the observed-factor and intercept parts shrink, and the dashed total never moves. Why: the observed factor and the intercept load on the second signal, and the more it overlaps book-to-market, where the hidden factor loads, the more of it the characteristic ruler credits to the hidden factor. 3. Switch to stock B: two parts are negative and grow more negative as ρ rises, yet the total stays at 0.20. A negative part means that source is credited with pulling the stock's expected return down. **What to notice:** the fit cannot tell you which bar is right; only the ruler decides.
:::

::: {#figure-csm-toy .column-body-outset .dfigure .toy role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-csm-toy-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-csm-toy-title"><strong>Figure 1: One fitted return, two rulers.</strong> Illustrative example, not paper data.</div>

{{< include /research/_fig-csm-toy.qmd >}}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Two characteristics (book-to-market and a second value signal), one hidden factor, one observed factor and an intercept. The top bar splits a stock's fitted return under the plain ruler; the bottom bar uses the characteristic ruler, under which the two signals overlap by ρ. The dashed tick marks the fitted return: 1.00 for stock A and 0.20 for stock B, under both rulers. The table's last column measures, with each ruler, how much the intercept carries; this is what a cap on the intercept limits. Real overlaps are mostly lower, with a median of 0.06 <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.1, p. 31">(p. 31)</span>; higher values are shown for visibility. In real data ρ is estimated, so every bar length inherits its estimation error; Figure 2 shows what happens to standard errors if you ignore it. <span class="provenance">Source: illustrative calculation using the matched transformation in the paper's Proposition 1 and equations 3.2 to 3.4; no data file.</span></div>
:::

Where the analogy differs: the characteristic ruler, once chosen, is computed from the characteristics, so its marks are drawn from the same data being measured. The matched change also alters the factor series, not only the shares <span class="loc" title="Paper, Proposition 1, p. 7">(Proposition 1, p. 7)</span>.

## Design and main results {#design-and-main-results}

The evidence has three parts <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8, pp. 30-38">(Section 8, pp. 30–38)</span>. A U.S. stock panel with 153 monthly characteristics, 1962–2025, measures how much real characteristics overlap <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.1, p. 30">(Section 8.1, p. 30)</span>. A stylised simulation ($L = 12$ characteristics, $N = 100$ stocks, 2,000 replications at $T = 240$ and $960$ time periods) holds the point estimate fixed and compares ways of computing standard errors <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.2, pp. 32-33">(pp. 32–33)</span>. A local experiment, a stylised simulation of the large-sample approximation that does not re-estimate a factor panel <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.3, p. 38">(p. 38)</span>, places the true value at set distances from an estimated cap on the intercept and compares intervals near it <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.3, pp. 35-36">(Section 8.3, pp. 35–36)</span>.

<div class="dfigure-title"><strong>Table 1: How 153 U.S. characteristics spread and overlap.</strong> The characteristic ruler, averaged over January 1962–December 2025 and trace-normalised, against the plain ruler <span class="loc" title="Paper, Table I, p. 31">(Table I, p. 31)</span>.</div>

::: {.table-scroll}
| Diagnostic | Characteristic ruler (Gram metric) | Plain ruler (identity) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Share of variation in the largest direction | 0.132 | 0.007 |
| Share in the five largest directions | 0.379 | 0.033 |
| Directions needed for 90% of variation | 68 | 138 |
| Mean absolute off-diagonal entry | 0.114 | 0.000 |
| Largest ÷ smallest eigenvalue | 2,339 | 1 |
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** Under the plain ruler, which treats the 153 as unrelated, 138 directions are needed to reach 90% of the variation. Measured by the stocks they pick out, 68 suffice <span class="loc" title="Paper, Table I, p. 31">(Table I, p. 31)</span>. On a scale where 0 means two signals' stock scores do not line up at all and 1 means they line up perfectly (an absolute cosine, not necessarily a correlation), most pairs barely overlap (median 0.06), but one pair in twenty exceeds 0.38 <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.1, p. 31">(p. 31)</span>. This describes exposure overlap, not the number of priced risks <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.1, p. 32">(p. 32)</span>.
:::

::: {#figure-csm-coverage .column-body-outset .dfigure role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-csm-coverage-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-csm-coverage-title"><strong>Figure 2: What is missed when the estimated ruler is treated as known.</strong> Same point estimate, five ways of computing standard errors, stylised simulation.</div>

{{< include /research/_fig-csm-coverage.qmd >}}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Rows are ways of computing standard errors (Table II, p. 34); circles and squares are two reported quantities, each measuring how closely a fixed combination of characteristics lines up with the hidden factors (true value 0.5). The top two rows ("Monte Carlo scale", "Oracle-influence HAC") need information available only in a simulation. Compare "Ruler treated as known" with "Complete-score HAC" (HAC: heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent), the paper's full method, which includes the ruler's error. The dashed line is the target: intervals that contain the true value 95 times in 100, or standard errors equal to the actual spread across replications. "Tail calibration" compares quantiles of the standardised estimate with normal quantiles at $T = 960$; the grey diagonal is a perfect fit. <span class="provenance">Source: paper Table II and Figure 2, and Section 8.2 for the paired gains; rebuilt_interior_coverage.csv, paired_coverage_gains.csv, studentized_quantiles.csv.</span> <a href="/data/csm_coverage.json">Data</a></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** In this stylised simulation with 960 time periods, treating the estimated ruler as known makes standard errors too small, so intervals meant to contain the true value 95 times in 100 contain it only about 89 and 92 times. Including the ruler's error restores about 94–95, with the same point estimates <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.2 and Table II, pp. 33-34">(Table II, p. 34)</span>. Most of the shortfall is the ruler's own variance <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.2, p. 33">(Section 8.2, p. 33)</span>; with 240 time periods even the complete method falls slightly short, at about 93–94 times.
:::

Near an estimated cap, the paper's stylised local experiment (960 time periods) again targets intervals that contain the true value 95 times in 100. One calibrated as if the cap binds contains it as few as about 84 times (83.80%) when the cap is in fact slack. One that holds whether or not the cap binds (the paper's drift-robust interval) contains it about 96–99 times (96.30–98.75%) at every tested distance <span class="loc" title="Paper, Table III, p. 36">(Table III, p. 36)</span>. The price is width: when the cap binds, it is about 25% wider (3.241 against 2.584) than a benchmark that knows how far the true value sits from the cap, which no one can compute in practice <span class="loc" title="Paper, Table III, p. 36; Section 8.3, p. 37">(Table III, p. 36)</span>.

## How it relates to prior work {#how-it-relates-to-prior-work}

Factor-model inference usually fixes rotation and scale by a normalisation. This paper asks what that normalisation does to the split when the ruler behind it is estimated from the data.

::: {.lit-table .table-scroll}
| Prior work | What it established | What this paper adds |
|---|---|---|
| @bai2003; @baing2013 | Identification and inference for large approximate factor models under normalisation restrictions. | Loadings identified up to hidden-factor rotations for each ruler, keeping observed-factor and intercept blocks; theory for a fixed cross section. |
| @kellypruittsu2019 | IPCA: characteristics set how strongly each stock moves with hidden factors, with an intercept and optional observed factors; rotation is fixed with the plain ruler, Γβ′Γβ = I. | Treats that normalisation as one choice of ruler, shows the split depends on it, and carries an estimated characteristic ruler into inference. |
| @newey1994; @neweymcfadden1994; @andrewsguggenberger2009; @andrewssoares2010 | First-step estimation corrections; uniformly valid inference when inequality constraints may bind. | Applies the two-step correction to a ruler that both selects the split and enters the report; near one smooth cap, uniform intervals from two endpoint calculations. |
:::

The angle is measurement, not a new predictor. The tools are known: geometry on matrix manifolds, two-step adjustment and constrained projection. What is new is their combination for one object, a split of fitted returns whose ruler is estimated from the same data and may also set the cap on the intercept.

<details class="robustness">
<summary>For specialists: further related work</summary>

Matrix-manifold geometry [@edelmanariassmith1998] removes hidden-factor rotations; boundary limit laws [@geyer1994; @andrews1999; @shapiro2000] are extended to a boundary learned through the same ruler; and where @li2025 bootstraps constrained estimators, this paper's route is analytic and uniform over local slack.

</details>

**Where it fits.** [Geometric Framework](/research/geometric-framework.html), an earlier and broader version of this paper, argued for taking the ruler from the data; this paper proves that the ruler decides how a fixed fit is split and shows how to do inference when the ruler is estimated. [Characteristic Geometry](/research/characteristic-geometry.html) cites it as its companion theory paper and follows a change of ruler into a portfolio; [Interpreting Pricing Errors](/research/interpreting-pricing-errors.html) cites it for the representation identities <span class="loc" title="Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors, p. 4">(p. 4)</span> and holds the ruler fixed to read alphas. The [job market paper](/research/characteristic-libraries.html), which also cites it as a companion paper, asks a parallel question about the library and the ridge penalty. Changing the library is not a change of ruler in this paper's sense.

## Scope {#scope}

- Better uncertainty measurement, not better fitted returns <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.2, p. 33">(Section 8.2, p. 33)</span>.
- The simulation is stylised, not calibrated to U.S. data <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 8.2, pp. 32-33">(pp. 32–33)</span>.
- Reading the intercept as a pricing error needs a specified pricing model <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 2, p. 5">(Section 2, p. 5)</span>.
- The ruler is a declared convention; no ruler is shown to be best <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 1, p. 2">(p. 2)</span>.
- Local, well-identified theory; near a cap, one smooth constraint and one reported number only <span class="loc" title="Paper, Section 7.3, p. 28; Section 7.4, p. 30; Section 9, p. 38">(Sections 7.3 and 9, pp. 28, 38)</span>.
